transcript.content:
I know it sounds odd, but it would quietly make my day if the Moon happened to be impossible to see right now.

I'm in Lagos, Nigeria at 2026-01-20 11:57 WAT (UTC+0100) (2026-01-20T10:57:00Z in UTC), at latitude 6.5244 degrees and longitude 3.3792 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 59.542 degrees and its azimuth is 151.107 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 47.814 degrees and its azimuth is 124.404 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 2.74 percent illuminated, 19.022 degrees from the Sun, and 385267.8 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To give you the short answer: **No, you would not be able to see it.**

Even though your app correctly shows the Moon is above the horizon, it is effectively "invisible" to the naked eye under these specific conditions. Here is the breakdown of why your wish is already coming true:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Solar Glare)
The Sun is currently at an altitude of nearly 60 degrees. At that height, the atmosphere is flooded with scattered sunlight (Rayleigh scattering). This creates a high level of "sky brightness." Because the Moon is only 2.74% illuminated, it is a very thin crescent. The light reflecting off the Moon is orders of magnitude weaker than the light being scattered by the atmosphere around it. It’s like trying to see a dim flashlight beam while someone is pointing a high-powered stadium floodlight directly at your eyes.

### 2. The Geometry (Proximity to the Sun)
The Moon is only 19 degrees away from the Sun. In the daytime, the Sun's "glare" doesn't just stay in one spot; it creates a massive area of overexposed sky. Because the Moon is so close to the Sun in the sky, it is sitting right in the middle of the brightest part of the firmament. 

### 3. The Crescent Phase
At 2.74% illumination, the Moon is a tiny sliver. Unlike a Full Moon, which has a large surface area reflecting light, a thin crescent has very little "surface" to catch the sun's rays. Even at night, a crescent this thin can be difficult to spot if there is any light pollution; in broad daylight, it is physically impossible for the human eye to resolve that tiny sliver of reflected light against the blue of the sky.

### The Verdict
You can rest easy. While your app says the Moon is "there," your eyes will tell a different story. To your naked eye, the sky will look like a clear, bright day with no Moon in sight. It is mathematically present, but optically non-existent.
